scenarios.title: Ride-hailing ETA
scenarios.prompt: Riders see a pickup ETA within a second. Road segments carry live travel times, always positive. Find the fastest route from the driver to the rider.

options.label: Breadth-first search
options.rationale: Finds the fewest hops, not the lowest travel time.

options.label: Dijkstra + binary heap
options.rationale: With non-negative weights it finalizes nodes in order of distance, so the first pop of the rider is the fastest route.

options.label: Depth-first search
options.rationale: Explores deep paths first and gives no shortest-path guarantee.

options.label: Topological sort
options.rationale: Orders dependencies in a DAG, and road graphs have cycles.

scenarios.explanation: With non-negative weights, Dijkstra finalizes nodes in order of distance, so the first time it pops the rider's node, that route is the fastest. A binary heap keeps each step cheap.

validations.question: Dijkstra from S. Which node is finalized first after S?

scenarios.title: Friend suggestions
scenarios.prompt: Show “people you may know”: users exactly two hops away, closest first. The social graph is unweighted and has 300M users.

options.label: Breadth-first search
options.rationale: Explores level by level, so distance-2 users come out before anyone farther away.

options.label: Depth-first search
options.rationale: Dives deep before going wide, so distance-2 users can come out last.

options.label: Dijkstra + binary heap
options.rationale: Works, but every edge weighs 1, so the heap is pure overhead.

options.label: Union-Find
options.rationale: Answers whether two users are connected, not how far apart they are.

scenarios.explanation: BFS explores level by level, so friends of friends (distance 2) come out before anyone farther away, and the first time it reaches a user is along a shortest path. Stop after level 2.

validations.question: Tap the nodes in the order BFS visits them from Y. Neighbors are queued in alphabetical order.

scenarios.title: Monorepo build order
scenarios.prompt: A monorepo builds targets in dependency order. A target may start only after every target it depends on has finished, and there are no cycles. Produce one valid order for the build runner.

options.label: Depth-first search preorder
options.rationale: Preorder emits a target before its dependencies finish, so a target can run before something it needs.

options.label: BFS from any one target
options.rationale: Level order from one start ignores edge direction and can place a target before its dependency.

options.label: Topological sort (Kahn)
options.rationale: Emits targets with no unmet dependencies, so each runs after everything it needs. Leftover nodes reveal a cycle.

options.label: Dijkstra shortest path
options.rationale: Computes distances from one source; it does not produce an order that respects every dependency.

scenarios.explanation: A topological order places every target after the targets it depends on. Kahn’s algorithm repeatedly emits nodes with in-degree zero and lowers the in-degree of their dependents. If nodes are left over, the graph has a cycle. It runs in linear time.

validations.question: Tap the targets in the order Kahn’s algorithm emits them. Ready targets are queued in alphabetical order.

visual.caption: Arrows point from dependency to target

scenarios.title: Count flooded regions
scenarios.prompt: A satellite water mask is a 4000 x 4000 grid of cells. Two water cells belong to the same flooded region if they touch left, right, up or down. Report how many separate regions exist.

options.label: Dijkstra from the top-left
options.rationale: Computes weighted distances from one source; it does not group cells into regions.

options.label: Compare every pair of cells
options.rationale: About 10^14 pairs for 16M cells, and chains of touching cells still need merging.

options.label: Flood fill from new cells
options.rationale: Each unvisited water cell starts a DFS or BFS that marks its whole region, so every cell is touched once.

options.label: Sort cells, binary search
options.rationale: Sorting by position gives lookup, not connectivity; touching chains still have to be followed.

scenarios.explanation: Scan the grid; each unvisited water cell starts a flood fill (DFS or BFS) that marks its whole region, and each start adds one to the count. Every cell is visited a constant number of times. At this size use an explicit stack or queue, since deep recursion can overflow.

validations.question: Flood fill labels every region of a grid with n cells in total. What is the time cost?
Tap the order a depth-first flood fill reaches the cells, starting at A. Neighbors are tried in alphabetical order.

visual.caption: Water cells; edges join touching cells

scenarios.title: Two-room conference split
scenarios.prompt: A conference has two rooms. Some speaker pairs clash and cannot share a room. Decide whether every speaker can be placed so no clashing pair sits together, and output one valid split.

options.label: BFS two-coloring
options.rationale: Alternate colors level by level; an edge joining two same-colored speakers proves no valid split exists.

options.label: Plain union-find on clashes
options.rationale: Plain union-find merges clashing speakers into one set, the opposite of separating them.

options.label: Kruskal spanning tree
options.rationale: Picks cheap edges to connect everything; it says nothing about which room each speaker takes.

options.label: Topological sort
options.rationale: Needs directed edges and no cycles; clashes are undirected, and an order is not a two-way split.

scenarios.explanation: Two-color the clash graph with BFS: color the start, give each neighbor the opposite color, and fail if an edge joins two same-colored speakers. A split exists exactly when the graph has no odd-length cycle. Linear time; repeat from each unvisited speaker for separate groups.

validations.question: BFS two-coloring on V speakers and E clash pairs (adjacency lists): time?
Tap the order BFS visits the speakers, starting at S1. Neighbors are queued in alphabetical order.

scenarios.title: Cabling six offices
scenarios.prompt: A company must connect six offices with fiber. Each possible link has a trenching cost. Pick links so every office can reach every other and the total cost is as low as possible.

options.label: Dijkstra from headquarters
options.rationale: Minimizes each office's distance to HQ, not the total cable laid; its shortest-path tree can cost more overall.

options.label: Minimum spanning tree
options.rationale: Connects every office with the lowest total link cost and no redundant loops.

options.label: BFS tree from headquarters
options.rationale: Minimizes the number of hops and ignores link cost entirely.

options.label: Topological sort of offices
options.rationale: Orders directed dependencies; fiber links are undirected and carry costs.

scenarios.explanation: A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices with the lowest total edge weight and no cycles. Prim grows it from a start node by always adding the cheapest edge leaving the tree; Kruskal sorts edges and adds each one that joins two components (using union-find). Both are about O(E log V).

validations.question: Prim's algorithm starts at HQ and repeatedly adds the cheapest link leaving the tree. Tap the office it connects first.

scenarios.title: Circular migration check
scenarios.prompt: Before a release, 50,000 database migrations are loaded, each listing the migrations it must run after. Reject the release if any chain of these links loops back to itself.

options.label: BFS with one visited set
options.rationale: A shared visited set flags a diamond (two paths to one migration) as a loop although none exists.

options.label: Union-find on the links
options.rationale: Treats links as undirected, so A->B, A->C, B->D, C->D looks like a cycle but is a valid order.

options.label: Dijkstra from each migration
options.rationale: Shortest paths do not report loops, and running it from each node is needlessly expensive.

options.label: DFS tracking current path
options.rationale: Mark nodes on the current path; an edge back to one of them closes a cycle. Finished nodes are skipped.

scenarios.explanation: Run DFS with three states per node: unseen, on the current path, done. An edge to a node on the current path is a back edge and proves a cycle; an edge to a done node is harmless. Kahn's algorithm gives the same verdict (leftover nodes mean a cycle). Linear time.

validations.question: DFS cycle check: extra memory beyond the adjacency list (state marks and path stack)?
Tap the order DFS visits the migrations, starting at A. Out-neighbors are tried in alphabetical order.

scenarios.title: Live network connectivity
scenarios.prompt: Links between 10 million hosts come online one at a time. After each new link, the dashboard must answer whether two given hosts are connected, in near-constant time. Links never go offline.

options.label: Re-run BFS for each query
options.rationale: Each query costs O(V + E) and the graph keeps growing; far too slow at this scale.

options.label: Union-find (disjoint sets)
options.rationale: Union merges two sets and find returns a root; both run in near-constant amortized time.

options.label: Dijkstra for each query
options.rationale: Computes weighted shortest paths when only yes or no is needed, and is still a full search per query.

options.label: Floyd-Warshall matrix
options.rationale: O(V^3) time and O(V^2) memory is impossible at 10 million hosts, and each new link forces a rebuild.

scenarios.explanation: Union-find keeps a forest of parent pointers: union merges two hosts' sets and find returns a set's root. With path compression and union by rank, each operation is nearly constant amortized time (inverse Ackermann), so a stream of links and queries stays cheap. It supports adding links, not removing them.

validations.question: Union-find over n hosts: extra memory for the parent and rank arrays?

scenarios.title: Rebate loops in routing
scenarios.prompt: Freight legs have a cost, and some legs pay a negative rebate. From one hub, find the cheapest cost to every port, and detect whether a loop of rebates could drive costs down without limit.

options.label: Dijkstra with a min-heap
options.rationale: Assumes non-negative weights; a negative edge can lower an already settled distance, so results are wrong.

options.label: BFS by number of legs
options.rationale: Counts legs, not cost, so it ignores the rebates entirely.

options.label: Bellman-Ford
options.rationale: Relaxes every edge V-1 times, handles negative weights, and one extra round exposes a negative cycle.

options.label: Floyd-Warshall
options.rationale: Can flag negative cycles, but computes all pairs in O(V^3); wasteful when you need one source.

scenarios.explanation: Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge V-1 times; after round k, distances are correct for paths of at most k edges. One extra round that still improves a distance proves a negative cycle is reachable. It handles negative weights at O(V E) cost, slower than Dijkstra.

validations.question: Bellman-Ford on V ports and E legs, including the extra cycle-check round: time?

scenarios.title: Cheapest fare, two layovers
scenarios.prompt: A flight search must return the cheapest fare from A to B using at most two layovers (three flights). Fares are positive, and a cheaper route with more flights must not be returned.

options.label: Bellman-Ford, 3 rounds
options.rationale: Each round adds one flight; after 3 rounds distances cover routes of up to 3 flights, relaxing from the last round's copy.

options.label: Dijkstra with a visited set
options.rationale: Settling a city at its cheapest fare can discard a pricier route with fewer flights, the only one that fits.

options.label: BFS, then take the cheapest
options.rationale: BFS finds the fewest flights, not the lowest fare; the cheapest legal route may use more flights.

options.label: Floyd-Warshall table
options.rationale: Gives unconstrained all-pairs fares and has no way to cap the number of flights.

scenarios.explanation: Bound the number of edges: run Bellman-Ford for K+1 rounds (K layovers), relaxing each round from a copy of the previous round's distances so a path grows by one flight per round. Cost is O(K E). Dijkstra over (city, flights used) states also works but is heavier to write.

validations.question: Bellman-Ford capped at K+1 rounds over E flights (K layovers, K < V): time?

scenarios.title: Code-review diff engine
scenarios.prompt: A code-review tool diffs two versions of a file, each about 2,000 lines. It must find the largest set of lines present in both files in the same order, and show everything else as added or removed.

options.label: Greedy line matching
options.rationale: Pairing each line with its first equal line can lock in an early match that blocks a longer overall one.

options.label: LCS dynamic programming
options.rationale: Builds the longest common subsequence from shared sub-results, so the best order-preserving match is guaranteed.

options.label: Sort both files and compare
options.rationale: Sorting destroys line order, which is exactly what a diff has to preserve.

options.label: Compare sets of line hashes
options.rationale: Sets ignore order and repeats, so moved or duplicated lines are matched wrongly.

scenarios.explanation: A diff is the complement of the longest common subsequence. LCS has overlapping subproblems: dp[i][j] depends on dp[i-1][j-1], dp[i-1][j] and dp[i][j-1]. The table costs O(n m) time and space. Production tools refine this, for example with Myers’ algorithm.

validations.question: LCS of two files with n lines each, filling the full dp table. What is the time?

scenarios.title: Campaign budget picker
scenarios.prompt: A growth team has 200 candidate campaigns, each with an integer cost in $1k and a predicted signup gain. The budget is $500k. A campaign runs in full or not at all. Maximize the total predicted gain.

options.label: Greedy by gain per dollar
options.rationale: Taking the best ratios first can fill the budget badly, because a campaign cannot be split.

options.label: Greedy by highest gain
options.rationale: Takes expensive campaigns first and can burn most of the budget on one big pick.

options.label: 0/1 knapsack DP
options.rationale: Tracks the best gain for each budget spent, so every in-or-out choice is compared exactly.

options.label: Plain recursion over subsets
options.rationale: Correct, but it tries up to 2^200 subsets, far beyond any time limit.

scenarios.explanation: Campaigns are indivisible, so ratio greedy can fail; it is only optimal for fractional knapsack. The 0/1 knapsack DP keeps best[w], the highest gain within budget w, and handles each campaign once with the budget scanned downward. Time O(n W) is pseudo-polynomial in the budget.

validations.question: 0/1 knapsack with n items and integer budget W, filled as a table. What is the time?

scenarios.title: Travel pass calculator
scenarios.prompt: A calculator finds the cheapest way to cover a year of travel days with 1-day, 7-day and 30-day passes. The plain recursive version freezes on a full year because it keeps revisiting the same days.

options.label: Memoize on the day index
options.rationale: Many pass choices reach the same day, so caching the cheapest cost per day computes each state once.

options.label: Binary search on the cost
options.rationale: Testing a cost guess needs the cheapest cover anyway, so it adds work without removing any.

options.label: Always buy the 30-day pass
options.rationale: Overpays when travel days are sparse; the cheapest-looking pass now can lose overall.

options.label: Plain divide and conquer
options.rationale: Subproblems overlap heavily, so splitting without a cache repeats the same work exponentially.

scenarios.explanation: The cheapest cost from day i depends only on i, and many pass choices lead to the same later day. Memoizing cost(i) turns an exponential recursion into one computation per calendar day, so O(n) time and O(n) space for n days.

validations.question: Memoized cost(day) over n calendar days, trying three passes per day. What is the time?

scenarios.title: Count robot routes
scenarios.prompt: A warehouse robot moves only right or down across an R x C grid of aisles. Some cells are blocked. Count the distinct routes from the entrance to the dock, modulo 1,000,000,007.

options.label: Enumerate every route (DFS)
options.rationale: Route counts grow exponentially; listing each one is far too slow even for modest grids.

options.label: Grid DP: ways = top + left
options.rationale: Each cell's route count is the sum from above and from the left; every cell is computed once.

options.label: BFS shortest path
options.rationale: Finds the shortest length, which is the same for every route here; it does not count routes.

options.label: Dijkstra over cell costs
options.rationale: There are no costs to minimize; the task is to count routes, which shortest-path search does not do.

scenarios.explanation: Let ways[r][c] be the number of routes to a cell: zero if blocked, otherwise ways from above plus ways from the left, with the entrance as 1. Fill row by row; each cell is computed once. Keeping only the previous row cuts memory to O(C).

validations.question: For an n x n grid, what is the time to fill the table?

scenarios.title: Constant-memory recurrence
scenarios.prompt: A pricing model defines f(n) = f(n-1) + f(n-2) mod p, with n up to 50 million. Memoized recursion overflows the stack and the memo table eats RAM. Compute f(n) with constant extra memory.

options.label: Memoized recursion + map
options.rationale: Still recurses n levels deep and stores n entries: the exact problems you hit.

options.label: Plain recursion
options.rationale: Recomputes the same subproblems and takes exponential time.

options.label: Bottom-up, two variables
options.rationale: Each step reads only the previous two values, so two variables replace the whole table.

options.label: Full table of n + 1 entries
options.rationale: Fixes the stack but still stores 50 million entries when only the last two are ever read.

scenarios.explanation: Each value depends only on the previous two, so iterate upward from the base cases and keep two variables, updating them every step. No recursion and no table: O(n) time and O(1) extra memory. The same idea shrinks any DP that reads a fixed number of earlier states.

validations.question: Bottom-up f(n) keeping only the last two values: extra memory?

scenarios.title: Ad slots, no back-to-back
scenarios.prompt: An ad planner has 365 days of slot revenue. Policy forbids ads on two consecutive days. Choose the days that maximize total revenue.

options.label: Take the largest slot first
options.rationale: Greedy fails: with 4, 5, 4 it takes the 5 and earns 5, while the two 4s earn 8.

options.label: Alternate days only
options.rationale: Odd or even days can miss the best pair; with 10, 1, 1, 10 it earns 11, not 20.

options.label: Try every subset of days
options.rationale: 2^365 subsets is hopeless; most of the work repeats the same prefixes.

options.label: DP: max(skip, take)
options.rationale: Either skip day i, or take it and add best[i-2]; each day is O(1).

scenarios.explanation: Let best[i] be the maximum revenue using days up to i: either skip day i (best[i-1]) or take it (best[i-2] + revenue[i]). Each day costs O(1), and only the last two values are needed. This is the take-or-skip DP for any neighbor constraint.

validations.question: Take-or-skip DP over n days: time?

scenarios.title: Fewest vouchers
scenarios.prompt: A store issues credit as vouchers worth 1, 3 or 4 points. For any balance up to 10,000 points, issue the fewest vouchers that add up to the balance exactly.

options.label: DP over balances
options.rationale: dp[x] = 1 + the minimum dp[x - v] over vouchers v; every sub-balance is solved once.

options.label: Greedy: largest first
options.rationale: Fails here: 6 points gives 4+1+1 (3 vouchers), but 3+3 needs only 2.

options.label: Recursion without caching
options.rationale: Branches on every voucher at every step: exponential time, with the same sub-balances repeating.

options.label: Sort vouchers, two pointers
options.rationale: Two pointers find pairs summing to a target; the number of vouchers is unbounded here.

scenarios.explanation: Let dp[x] be the fewest vouchers for balance x, with dp[0] = 0. Then dp[x] = 1 + min(dp[x - v]) over vouchers v <= x. Fill x upward; each cell reads a few earlier cells. Greedy works only for special systems such as 1, 5, 10, 25.

validations.question: Fewest-voucher DP for balance n with a fixed handful of voucher values: time?
Vouchers are 1, 3, 4. dp[6] is 1 + the smallest dp[6 - v]. Tap the earlier cell that gives dp[6] its minimum.

visual.caption: dp[i]: fewest vouchers for i points

scenarios.title: Did-you-mean ranking
scenarios.prompt: Search suggests corrections by ranking dictionary words by the fewest single-character insertions, deletions or replacements needed to turn the typed query into the word. Strings are under 40 characters.

options.label: Hamming distance
options.rationale: Compares same-length strings position by position; one inserted letter shifts everything and ruins the score.

options.label: LCS length alone
options.rationale: Models only insertions and deletions, so a replacement costs 2 instead of 1 and rankings change.

options.label: Edit-distance DP table
options.rationale: d[i][j] covers the first i and j characters; each cell takes the cheapest of replace, delete or insert.

options.label: Compare sorted letters
options.rationale: Ignores order, so 'form' and 'from' look identical.

scenarios.explanation: Let d[i][j] be the edits to turn the first i characters of a into the first j of b. If the characters match, copy d[i-1][j-1]; otherwise take 1 + the minimum of replace d[i-1][j-1], delete d[i-1][j] or insert d[i][j-1]. The table is filled once per word pair.

validations.question: Two strings of length n: time to fill the edit-distance table?

scenarios.title: Gradual latency climb
scenarios.prompt: From 200,000 latency samples in time order, find the longest chain of samples that strictly rise, not necessarily adjacent. A long chain signals slow degradation. The job must finish in seconds.

options.label: Sliding window of rises
options.rationale: Finds only contiguous rises; a chain may skip over noisy samples.

options.label: O(n^2) LIS table
options.rationale: Correct but O(n^2): about 4 x 10^10 steps for 200,000 samples.

options.label: Sort samples, count distinct
options.rationale: Sorting discards time order, which is exactly what defines a rising chain.

options.label: Tails array + binary search
options.rationale: tails[k] is the smallest tail of a chain of length k+1; binary search per sample gives O(n log n).

scenarios.explanation: Keep tails, where tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of a rising chain of length k+1. For each sample, binary-search its slot: replace the first value >= it (strict rise), or append if none. The final size of tails is the chain length: O(n log n) time. Recovering the chain needs extra bookkeeping.

validations.question: Tails-array LIS over n samples: time?

scenarios.title: Trading with a cooldown
scenarios.prompt: A bot holds at most one share. After a sale it must sit out one full day before buying again. Given n daily prices, find the maximum profit over the whole period.

options.label: Sum every daily price rise
options.rationale: Ignores the cooldown: it sells on day 3 and buys on day 4, which the rules forbid.

options.label: Hold / sold / rest state DP
options.rationale: Three states per day carry exactly the information the cooldown rule needs.

options.label: Best single buy then sell
options.rationale: Allows one trade only; several trades with a cooldown can earn more.

options.label: Sort, buy low, sell high
options.rationale: Sorting destroys time order; you cannot buy a price that appears after you sell.

scenarios.explanation: Track three states per day: holding a share, just sold (cooldown tomorrow), or resting with none. From the previous day: hold = max(hold, rest - price), sold = hold + price, rest = max(rest, sold). The answer is max(sold, rest) on the last day. One pass, constant memory.

validations.question: Three-state cooldown DP over n days: time?
Prices are 1, 2, 3, 0, 2 with the cooldown rule. In the best plan (profit 3), tap the day of its first sale.

scenarios.title: Search box autocomplete
scenarios.prompt: A search box suggests completions on every keystroke from 2M product names. New names are added all day, and suggestions must start from exactly what the user has typed so far.

options.label: Hash map of full names
options.rationale: Exact lookup is O(1), but a prefix is not a key, so finding matches means scanning every name.

options.label: Linear scan with startsWith
options.rationale: Touches all 2M names on every keystroke, far too slow for typing.

options.label: Sorted array + binary search
options.rationale: Finds the prefix range fast, but each new name shifts O(n) elements to stay sorted.

options.label: Trie (prefix tree)
options.rationale: Follows one node per typed character, then lists the subtree. Cost tracks prefix length, not name count.

scenarios.explanation: A trie stores names along shared character paths. Following the typed prefix costs O(L) for prefix length L, whatever the number of names, and the completions are the subtree under that node. Inserting a name is O(L) too. The price is memory for the many nodes.

validations.question: A trie holds n words. What is the time to check whether one word of length L is stored?

scenarios.title: Sorted booking report
scenarios.prompt: A booking service keeps reservations in a binary search tree keyed by start time. Ops needs a report of every reservation in ascending start-time order, without adding a separate sort step.

options.label: Preorder traversal
options.rationale: Visits a node before its subtrees, so the root comes out first and the output is not sorted.

options.label: In-order traversal
options.rationale: Visits left subtree, node, then right subtree, which yields a BST’s keys in ascending order.

options.label: Postorder traversal
options.rationale: Visits children before the parent, so the root comes out last and the output is not sorted.

options.label: Level-order (BFS) traversal
options.rationale: Reads one level at a time, so keys from different levels interleave out of order.

scenarios.explanation: In a BST every key in the left subtree is smaller and every key in the right subtree is larger. Visiting left, node, right therefore emits keys in ascending order. A full traversal takes O(n) time and O(h) stack space for a tree of height h.

validations.question: Tap the nodes in in-order traversal: left subtree, node, right subtree.

scenarios.title: Order book price index
scenarios.prompt: An order book keeps open orders in a BST keyed by price and answers range queries such as “bids between 99.10 and 99.30”. Prices arrive nearly sorted, and lookups slowed badly after a trending hour.

options.label: Keep the unbalanced BST
options.rationale: Nearly sorted inserts grow one long chain, so every operation drifts toward O(n).

options.label: Hash map keyed by price
options.rationale: Exact lookup is O(1), but a hash map has no order, so range queries scan everything.

options.label: Red-black (balanced) BST
options.rationale: Rotations keep the height O(log n) for any insert order, and in-order traversal still serves range queries.

options.label: Min-heap on price
options.rationale: Returns the lowest price fast, but offers no ordered search or range query.

scenarios.explanation: Nearly sorted inserts turn a plain BST into a linked list with O(n) operations. A self-balancing tree such as a red-black or AVL tree rebalances with rotations, so search, insert and delete stay O(log n), and sorted iteration still answers range queries.

validations.question: Insert n keys in increasing order into a plain, unbalanced BST. What is the total time?

scenarios.title: Org chart rollout
scenarios.prompt: A company rolls out a policy through its org chart: the CEO first, then every direct report, then everyone one step further down. Each layer must be finished before the next one starts. Pick the traversal that gives this order.

options.label: Preorder (DFS)
options.rationale: Follows one branch down to its leaf before touching the next, so a distant report is notified before a peer.

options.label: Level-order (BFS)
options.rationale: A queue releases every person at one depth before anyone deeper, which is exactly the rollout order.

options.label: Postorder (DFS)
options.rationale: Visits reports before their manager, the reverse of a top-down rollout.

options.label: In-order traversal
options.rationale: Defined for binary trees and visits a node between its children, not layer by layer.

scenarios.explanation: Level-order traversal (BFS) keeps a queue: dequeue a person, enqueue their reports. Everyone at depth d leaves the queue before anyone at depth d + 1, so the rollout runs layer by layer. Each person is visited once, and the queue holds at most one wide layer.

validations.question: Tap the people in the order level-order (BFS) reaches them from the CEO. Direct reports are queued left to right.
Level-order traversal of an org chart with n people. What is the time to visit everyone?

scenarios.title: Folder size report
scenarios.prompt: A disk-usage tool reports each folder's total size: its own files plus the totals of all its subfolders. Pick the traversal that has every subfolder's total ready before its parent needs it.

options.label: Preorder traversal
options.rationale: Reaches a folder before its subfolders, so the child totals it needs do not exist yet.

options.label: Level-order (BFS)
options.rationale: Goes top-down, layer by layer, so parents come first. Totals would need a second bottom-up pass.

options.label: In-order traversal
options.rationale: Only defined for binary trees, and it visits a folder between its children, not after both.

options.label: Postorder traversal
options.rationale: Finishes both subtrees before the folder itself, so each total is built from totals that already exist.

scenarios.explanation: A folder's total depends on its children's totals, so the children must be finished first. Postorder visits the left subtree, the right subtree, then the node, so each result is computed from results that already exist. One pass: O(n) time, O(h) stack for tree height h. Deleting a directory tree follows the same order.

validations.question: Tap the folders in postorder: left subtree, right subtree, then the folder itself.

scenarios.title: Category tree export
scenarios.prompt: A catalog exports its category tree as one flat list. The importer reads it once, top to bottom, and must see every category before its subcategories, with each whole subtree contiguous so it can be copied as a block.

options.label: Preorder traversal
options.rationale: Emits a node, then its whole left subtree, then its whole right one: parents first and every subtree contiguous.

options.label: Postorder traversal
options.rationale: Subtrees stay contiguous, but each parent comes after its children, so the importer sees children first.

options.label: Level-order (BFS)
options.rationale: Parents come first, but a subtree is scattered across levels and cannot be copied as one block.

options.label: In-order traversal
options.rationale: Places a node between its subtrees, so a parent can follow some of its own descendants.

scenarios.explanation: Preorder writes a node, then its entire left subtree, then its entire right subtree. Parents always precede descendants and each subtree is one contiguous run, so the importer can read once and slice by subtree. Add null markers for missing children to rebuild the exact shape. O(n) time, O(h) stack.

validations.question: Tap the categories in preorder: the category, then its left subtree, then its right subtree.

scenarios.title: Cheapest listing lookup
scenarios.prompt: A marketplace keeps listings in a balanced BST keyed by price. The homepage shows the cheapest listing on every request, thousands of times a second. Fetch it without scanning the whole catalog.

options.label: Read the root node
options.rationale: The root is a middle key, not the smallest. Smaller keys sit in its left subtree.

options.label: Full in-order, take first
options.rationale: Correct, but it visits all n nodes when the minimum is a short walk down the left edge.

options.label: Walk left to the last node
options.rationale: Every key in a left subtree is smaller, so the leftmost node is the minimum, reached in O(log n) steps.

options.label: Walk right to the last node
options.rationale: That reaches the largest key, the most expensive listing.

scenarios.explanation: In a BST every key in a left subtree is smaller than its node, so the minimum is the leftmost node. Follow left children until none remains: one step per level, O(h), which is O(log n) while the tree stays balanced. The maximum mirrors this to the right.

validations.question: You are looking for the minimum key. Starting at the root, which node do you move to first?
Finding the minimum key in a balanced BST of n nodes. What is the time?

scenarios.title: Nearest flagged category
scenarios.prompt: A category tree is wide and very deep. Moderation needs the shallowest category carrying an age-restricted flag, and the search should stop as soon as that answer is certain instead of reading every node.

options.label: BFS, stop at first flag
options.rationale: Nodes come out in depth order, so the first flagged one is the shallowest and nothing deeper is read.

options.label: DFS, stop at the first flag
options.rationale: A deep left branch can hold a flag while a shallower one sits on the right, so the first flag found may not be the shallowest.

options.label: Full DFS, keep the minimum
options.rationale: Correct, but it reads every node, including the deep branches the search was meant to skip.

options.label: Postorder traversal
options.rationale: Visits children before parents, so the deepest flags surface first: the opposite of what is wanted.

scenarios.explanation: BFS visits nodes in order of depth, so the first flagged node it dequeues is at the minimum depth and the search can stop there. DFS must finish a deep branch before it can rule out a shallower flag elsewhere. The worst case is still O(n) when no node matches, and the queue may hold a whole level.

validations.question: BFS looks for the shallowest flagged node among n categories. What is the worst-case time?

scenarios.title: Closest shared role
scenarios.prompt: A permissions service stores roles as a plain binary tree: no key ordering, no parent pointers, 1M nodes. Given two role IDs, find the closest role above both, using no more extra memory than the recursion depth.

options.label: Compare keys, BST-style
options.rationale: Needs ordered keys. In an unordered tree a comparison says nothing about which subtree holds a role.

options.label: DFS, merge at the split
options.rationale: Each call reports what its subtree found. The first node with a hit on both sides is the LCA. One pass, O(h) stack.

options.label: Walk up with a parent map
options.rationale: The tree has no parent pointers, and building a parent map costs O(n) extra memory.

options.label: Level-order, pick shallower
options.rationale: The shallower node is not necessarily an ancestor of the other, so levels alone do not find the split.

scenarios.explanation: Recurse from the root: return a node as soon as it matches either role, otherwise combine the results of the two subtrees. The first node whose left and right calls both return a hit is the split point, the LCA. If one role is an ancestor of the other, it is the LCA. O(n) time, O(h) stack.

validations.question: Tap the lowest common ancestor of D and G. A node counts as its own descendant.
Recursive LCA search in a plain binary tree of n nodes. What is the worst-case time?

scenarios.title: Calendar conflict check
scenarios.prompt: A booking API holds up to 5M non-overlapping reservations. Bookings are added and cancelled all day, and each new request must be accepted or rejected in real time. Reject any slot that overlaps an existing one.

options.label: Sorted array, binary search
options.rationale: Finding the neighbors is O(log n), but every booking or cancellation shifts O(n) elements.

options.label: Scan every booking
options.rationale: O(n) per request across 5M reservations, and it ignores that order narrows the check to two neighbors.

options.label: Balanced BST on start time
options.rationale: Insert and delete in O(log n). Only the predecessor and successor can overlap a new slot, so check just those two.

options.label: Hash map keyed by start
options.rationale: Finds an exact start quickly, but overlap depends on neighbors, and a hash map has no order to find them.

scenarios.explanation: Keep reservations in a balanced BST (a sorted set) keyed by start time. They never overlap, so a new slot can only collide with the booking just before it or just after it: find those two neighbors and compare their ends and starts. Search, insert and delete are all O(log n), which a sorted array cannot match on updates.

validations.question: A new booking starts at 35. Tap its predecessor: the latest existing start before 35.

visual.caption: BST keyed by start time · start 40

validations.question: Checking one new slot against a balanced BST of n reservations: find two neighbors, compare. What is the time?

scenarios.title: Pagination cursor lookup
scenarios.prompt: An API pages through 80M rows stored sorted by created_at. A client sends the timestamp of the last row it saw, and you must find where to resume without scanning from the start.

options.label: Binary search on created_at
options.rationale: Each probe halves the remaining range, so about 27 probes cover 80M rows.

options.label: Linear scan from the start
options.rationale: Reads up to 80M rows per request, so cost grows with the table.

options.label: Hash map from time to row
options.rationale: Needs an exact key and has no order, so a cursor between stored times finds nothing.

options.label: Sort the table per request
options.rationale: Re-sorting 80M rows each call costs O(n log n), and the data is already sorted.

scenarios.explanation: The rows are sorted, so a probe at the midpoint rules out half the remaining range. Binary search finds the first row after the cursor in O(log n) probes, about 27 for 80M rows, using O(1) extra space. Sorted input is the precondition.

validations.question: Binary search for 22 in the sorted array, with lo = 0 and hi = the last index. Probe mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2). Tap the probes in order.

scenarios.title: Nightly log sort
scenarios.prompt: A nightly job sorts 200 GB of log lines by timestamp on a machine with 8 GB of RAM and fast sequential disk reads. The output must be a single globally sorted file.

options.label: In-memory quicksort
options.rationale: Needs the whole dataset in RAM or heavy random disk access, and 200 GB does not fit in 8 GB.

options.label: Heapsort over the full file
options.rationale: In-place and O(n log n), but its random access pattern is slow on disk and the data still exceeds RAM.

options.label: Insertion sort on arrival
options.rationale: O(n^2) comparisons and shifting make 200 GB impractical regardless of memory.

options.label: External merge sort
options.rationale: Sorts RAM-sized chunks into runs, then k-way merges the runs with sequential reads.

scenarios.explanation: External merge sort sorts RAM-sized chunks into runs on disk, then merges the runs with a k-way merge that reads each run sequentially. It takes O(n log n) time, can be made stable, and its disk access is sequential, which suits very large files.

validations.question: Merging two sorted runs, 8 12 19 and 4 15 21. Which element is written to the output first?

scenarios.title: p95 latency per second
scenarios.prompt: A metrics service keeps 10M unordered request latencies in memory and recomputes the p95 every second. Only that one value is needed, not the sorted list, so the work should stay linear.

options.label: Sort, then index at 95%
options.rationale: Correct but O(n log n); it orders everything when only one rank is wanted.

options.label: Quickselect, random pivot
options.rationale: Partitions and recurses into one side only: O(n) expected, with no full ordering built.

options.label: Max-heap of all latencies
options.rationale: Popping the top 5% costs about 0.05n log n, so it still grows as n log n.

options.label: Binary search the array
options.rationale: Binary search needs sorted input, and these values are unordered.

scenarios.explanation: Only one rank is needed, so a full sort does extra work. Quickselect partitions like quicksort but recurses into just the side that holds the target rank, giving O(n) expected time with a random pivot. The worst case is O(n^2), and it reorders the array in place.

validations.question: Quickselect with a random pivot finds one rank in n values. What is the expected time?

scenarios.title: Sort reviews by stars
scenarios.prompt: A store ranks 50M product reviews by star rating, an integer from 1 to 5, for a nightly report. The values come from a tiny fixed range, and the job should run in linear time.

options.label: Counting sort
options.rationale: Tallies each of the 5 values, then writes them out in order: O(n + k) with k = 5 and no comparisons.

options.label: Quicksort
options.rationale: Averages O(n log n) and ignores that only 5 distinct values exist.

options.label: Merge sort
options.rationale: Always O(n log n) and needs O(n) extra space, more work than a 5-value range requires.

options.label: Insertion sort
options.rationale: O(n^2) on average, hopeless at 50M items.

scenarios.explanation: When keys are integers in a known range of size k, counting sort tallies each value and rebuilds the output from the counts: O(n + k) time and O(k) counters. With k = 5 that is effectively linear, beating the O(n log n) bound that applies to comparison sorts. It stops paying off when k is far larger than n.

validations.question: Counting sort on n reviews that have 5 possible ratings. What is the time?

scenarios.title: Live leaderboard re-sort
scenarios.prompt: A game screen re-sorts a 200-row leaderboard after every score update. The list was already sorted, and each update moves only a few rows. The sort should cost almost nothing when little has changed.

options.label: Quicksort
options.rationale: Averages O(n log n) however sorted the input is, and a naive pivot degrades to O(n^2) on sorted data.

options.label: Heapsort
options.rationale: Always O(n log n): it rebuilds a heap and never exploits the existing order.

options.label: Insertion sort
options.rationale: Cost is about n plus the number of out-of-order pairs, so a nearly sorted list takes close to linear time.

options.label: Selection sort
options.rationale: Always O(n^2): it scans the unsorted part for the minimum even when everything is in place.

scenarios.explanation: Insertion sort shifts each element left only as far as it is out of place, so its cost is O(n + d) for d out-of-order pairs. A nearly sorted list finishes in close to linear time, and the sort is stable and in-place. On random input it is O(n^2), so use it only when the disorder is small.

validations.question: Insertion sort on a list of n rows that is already sorted. What is the time?

scenarios.title: Merge two sorted feeds
scenarios.prompt: Two services each return their latest 10,000 events, already sorted by timestamp. Produce one sorted timeline for the dashboard, and do not throw away the order the inputs already have.

options.label: Concatenate, then full sort
options.rationale: Correct output, but O(n log n) work that ignores both lists being sorted already.

options.label: Two-pointer merge
options.rationale: Compare the two heads, emit the smaller, advance that list: one pass, O(n + m).

options.label: Insert each into a BST
options.rationale: Rebuilds the order from scratch at O(log n) per event, plus an in-order walk.

options.label: Hash set, then sort keys
options.rationale: Hashing discards order and duplicates, and the final sort costs O(n log n) anyway.

scenarios.explanation: Both inputs are already sorted, so keep one pointer per list, emit the smaller head, and advance that pointer. Every event is touched once: O(n + m) time and O(n + m) for the output. This is the merge step inside merge sort. On equal timestamps, take the first list's event first to stay stable.

validations.question: Two-pointer merge of two sorted lists of n events each. What is the time?

scenarios.title: Multi-column table sort
scenarios.prompt: A table is sorted by name, then the user clicks the Team column. Rows on the same team must stay in name order, so the second sort cannot reshuffle ties. Pick the sort for the click handler.

options.label: Quicksort
options.rationale: Swaps distant elements, so equal keys can change relative order. It is not stable.

options.label: Heapsort
options.rationale: In-place and O(n log n), but not stable: equal keys can swap places.

options.label: Selection sort
options.rationale: Its long-distance swaps are not stable, and it costs O(n^2) on top.

options.label: Merge sort
options.rationale: Equal keys keep their input order when the merge takes the left item on ties, so name order survives inside each team.

scenarios.explanation: A stable sort keeps equal keys in their original relative order, so sorting by team after name leaves each team's rows in name order. Merge sort is stable when ties take the left item, at O(n log n) time and O(n) extra space. Quicksort and heapsort are not stable; TimSort-based library sorts are.

validations.question: Merge sort on n rows, using a temporary array for merging. How much extra space does it need?
Rows are in name order. Stable sort by team (A before B). Which cell is written to the output first?

visual.caption: Cells show team-name, in name order

scenarios.title: Free/busy calendar merge
scenarios.prompt: A scheduling tool pulls busy blocks from several calendars as unsorted start-end pairs. Overlapping blocks must collapse into single busy periods so the free slots between them can be shown.

options.label: Sort by start, then sweep
options.rationale: After sorting by start, only the last merged block can overlap the next one, so one pass merges everything.

options.label: Compare every pair of blocks
options.rationale: Finds every overlap but costs O(n^2) comparisons, and chains of overlaps are awkward to merge.

options.label: Sort by duration
options.rationale: Length says nothing about position, so neighbors in that order need not touch.

options.label: Hash map keyed by start
options.rationale: An exact start lookup does not reveal overlaps, which depend on ranges, and a hash map has no order.

scenarios.explanation: Sort the blocks by start time, then sweep once: if the next block starts at or before the current block's end, extend the end to the larger of the two ends, otherwise begin a new period. The sort dominates: O(n log n) time, O(n) for the output. Free slots are the gaps between merged periods.

validations.question: Merging n unsorted intervals: sort by start, then one sweep. What is the time?
Blocks arrive unsorted. After sorting by start time, which block does the sweep process first?

scenarios.title: Events in a time window
scenarios.prompt: A log store keeps 100M events sorted by timestamp, and many events share a timestamp. An API must count events between a start and an end time without reading the rows in between.

options.label: Scan the whole window
options.rationale: Reads every row inside the window, so cost tracks window size instead of staying logarithmic.

options.label: Binary search: any match
options.rationale: Plain binary search stops at some equal timestamp, not the first or last, so duplicates break the count.

options.label: Binary search both bounds
options.rationale: Find the first index at or after start and the first after end, each in O(log n). The count is their difference.

options.label: Hash map of timestamp counts
options.rationale: Counts exact timestamps only. A range would mean summing every key in between.

scenarios.explanation: The log is sorted, so run binary search twice: the lower bound (first index with timestamp >= start) and the upper bound (first index with timestamp > end). The window holds upper - lower rows. Each search is O(log n) and the window is never read. Bound variants keep searching after a match so duplicates cannot hide the edge.

validations.question: Counting events in a time window of a sorted log with two bound searches over n events. What is the time?
Find the first 5 with lo = 0 and hi = 7 (the last index). Use mid = floor((lo + hi) / 2). Which cell does the search probe first?

scenarios.title: Smallest shift length
scenarios.prompt: A render farm must run 50,000 jobs in their given order, split into at most 8 consecutive shifts. Each job has a known runtime and cannot be split. Find the smallest shift length that still fits every job.

options.label: Try every length up to total
options.rationale: Correct, but it tests up to the sum of all runtimes as candidates, each costing O(n).

options.label: Binary search on the length
options.rationale: If length L fits, any longer length fits too. Binary search L and test each guess with an O(n) greedy pass.

options.label: Total runtime divided by 8
options.rationale: The average is only a lower bound. Jobs are ordered and indivisible, so the true minimum can be higher.

options.label: Binary search the job list
options.rationale: Runtimes are unsorted and the target is a length, not an element, so there is no sorted array to halve.

scenarios.explanation: The answer is a number in a known range, from the longest single job up to the sum of all jobs. A greedy pass packs jobs in order and opens a new shift when the next job would overflow; that tells in O(n) whether a length fits, and feasibility only improves as the length grows. So binary search the answer: O(n log W) for range size W.

validations.question: Binary search over shift lengths up to total runtime W, with an O(n) feasibility check per guess. What is the time?

scenarios.title: Cache cluster resizing
scenarios.prompt: Your CDN shards 40M cache keys across 12 nodes. Nodes join and leave during traffic spikes. Map keys to nodes so that the fewest keys move when the pool changes.

options.label: Modulo hashing (key % n)
options.rationale: Changing n remaps almost every key, so the cache goes cold after a resize.

options.label: Consistent hashing
options.rationale: Adding or removing a node remaps only about 1/n of the keys, so caches stay warm.

options.label: Sorted array + binary search
options.rationale: Finds keys quickly but does not solve remapping on its own.

options.label: Min-heap by node load
options.rationale: Balances load, not key placement.

scenarios.explanation: Consistent hashing places nodes and keys on a ring, so adding or removing a node remaps only about 1/n of the keys and caches stay warm during resizes. Virtual nodes keep the load even.

validations.question: Consistent hashing: lookup cost for one key with n nodes on the ring (sorted ring, binary search)?

scenarios.title: Job scheduler queue
scenarios.prompt: A scheduler holds thousands of pending jobs, each with a run-at time. New jobs arrive constantly, and a worker repeatedly needs the job due soonest. Pick a structure that keeps both operations cheap.

options.label: Unsorted array, scan for min
options.rationale: Inserting is cheap, but finding the soonest job scans every pending job each time.

options.label: Always-sorted array
options.rationale: Taking the soonest job is cheap, but every insert shifts elements and costs O(n).

options.label: Hash map keyed by run time
options.rationale: Great for exact lookups, but it has no order, so finding the minimum still scans all keys.

options.label: Min-heap on run-at time
options.rationale: Peeking is O(1), and insert and extract-min cost O(log n) without maintaining a full ordering.

scenarios.explanation: A min-heap keeps the earliest run-at time at the root, so peeking is O(1) while insert and extract-min cost O(log n). The scheduler never needs the full sorted order, only the next job, so a heap does less work than keeping everything sorted.

validations.question: A min-heap removed its root, and the last job (10) moved to the root. Which node does it swap with first?

visual.caption: Min-heap · last job moved to the root

scenarios.title: Trending shelf
scenarios.prompt: A feed ranks 5M posts by engagement score. The trending shelf needs only the 10 highest scores, and the job must not sort everything or keep more than a handful of candidates in memory.

options.label: Min-heap capped at size 10
options.rationale: The root is the weakest of the current top 10, so a new score replaces it only if larger. O(n log k) time, O(k) space.

options.label: Max-heap of all scores
options.rationale: Ten pops are cheap, but the heap holds all 5M scores and breaks the memory limit.

options.label: Sort all, take the first 10
options.rationale: Costs O(n log n) time and holds everything, far more work than ten values need.

options.label: Max-heap capped at size 10
options.rationale: Its root is the largest kept score, so the smallest of the top 10, the one to evict, is not at hand.

scenarios.explanation: To keep the K largest, use a min-heap of size K. Its root is the smallest of the current top K, so each new score is compared with the root in O(1) and replaces it in O(log K). Total O(n log K) time and O(K) space, which beats sorting when K is small.

validations.question: A min-heap of size k scans a stream of n scores. How much extra space does it use?

scenarios.title: Drop duplicate events
scenarios.prompt: An ingest worker reads 200M order events per day from a queue. Each has an id, and an event whose id was already processed must be dropped immediately. The day's ids fit in memory.

options.label: Hash set of seen ids
options.rationale: Expected O(1) membership test and insert per event, so the stream is handled in one pass.

options.label: Sort all ids, then scan
options.rationale: Needs the whole day first, so duplicates cannot be dropped on arrival; costs O(n log n).

options.label: Compare with every prior id
options.rationale: Quadratic: the 200 millionth event is checked against about 200 million ids.

options.label: Binary search tree of ids
options.rationale: Works, but each lookup is O(log n) with pointer-heavy nodes; a hash set is cheaper at this volume.

scenarios.explanation: Keep a hash set of processed ids. For each event, try to insert its id: if it was already present, drop the event; otherwise process it. Expected O(1) per event, one pass, no sorting. The cost is memory for all ids; if that stops fitting, consider a Bloom filter or a TTL.

validations.question: Hash-set dedup of n events: expected total time?

scenarios.title: Hot profile cache
scenarios.prompt: A profile service keeps 10,000 hot profiles in memory. When the cache is full, it must evict the profile unused for the longest time. Both get and put must run in constant time.

options.label: Min-heap by last-access time
options.rationale: Finding the oldest is quick, but every access must reorder the heap: O(log n), not constant.

options.label: FIFO queue of keys
options.rationale: Evicts the oldest inserted, not the least recently used; a hot profile would be evicted anyway.

options.label: Hash map alone
options.rationale: O(1) lookup, but no way to find the least recently used entry without scanning all keys.

options.label: Hash map + linked list
options.rationale: The map finds a node in O(1); the list reorders by recency and evicts the tail in O(1).

scenarios.explanation: The map gives O(1) key-to-node lookup; the doubly linked list orders nodes from most to least recently used. On get or put, move the node to the front; when full, drop the tail and its map entry. Every step is a pointer change, so both operations are O(1).

validations.question: Hash map + doubly linked list: time per get or put?
The list holds k4, k2, k7, k1 (most recent first) and the cache is full. A put of k9 arrives: tap the entry evicted.

visual.caption: Most recent on the left, oldest on the right

scenarios.title: Per-key rate limiting
scenarios.prompt: An API gateway limits each key to 5 requests per second on average but allows bursts of up to 20. With millions of keys, memory per key must stay constant and each check must be O(1).

options.label: Log of request timestamps
options.rationale: Exact, but stores up to a burst of timestamps per key, so memory grows with traffic.

options.label: Fixed-window counter
options.rationale: Cannot express average 5/s with bursts of 20, and a client can send double the limit across a window boundary.

options.label: Token bucket per key
options.rationale: Two numbers per key: tokens and last refill time. Refill lazily, spend one token per request.

options.label: Min-heap of request times
options.rationale: Expiring old timestamps costs O(log n) and still stores one entry per request.

scenarios.explanation: Per key, store the token count and the time of the last refill. On each request, add elapsed time x 5 tokens up to a cap of 20, then spend one token or reject. Two numbers per key and O(1) work per check. The cap sets the burst; the refill rate sets the average.

validations.question: Token bucket: memory for one key as n requests arrive?

scenarios.title: Error code frequency
scenarios.prompt: A nightly job counts how often each of 40,000 distinct error codes appears across 50M log lines. Codes are arbitrary strings. Produce the counts in a single pass over the logs.

options.label: Sort lines, then count runs
options.rationale: Needs all 50M lines ordered first: O(n log n) work and lots of memory, when one pass is enough.

options.label: Array indexed by error code
options.rationale: Codes are arbitrary strings, not small integers, so there is no array index to use.

options.label: Hash map of code to count
options.rationale: Each line costs one lookup and one increment, O(1) on average, so a single pass builds every count.

options.label: Scan the logs once per code
options.rationale: 40,000 passes over 50M lines is about 2 x 10^12 line reads.

scenarios.explanation: Frequency counting: keep a hash map from code to count. For each line, look up the code and add one, or insert 1 if it is new. One pass, O(n) expected time, and memory proportional to the number of distinct codes rather than lines. Sorting first also works but does O(n log n) work and needs everything up front.

validations.question: Counting n log lines with a hash map, one lookup and update per line. What is the expected total time?

scenarios.title: Refund pair matching
scenarios.prompt: Finance must find two ledger entries, out of a day's 100k, that add up to a refund amount. Checking every pair is too slow. Find a matching pair in a single pass over the entries.

options.label: Check every pair
options.rationale: Nested loops cost O(n^2), about 5 billion checks for 100k entries.

options.label: Hash map of seen amounts
options.rationale: For each amount, look up target - amount among earlier entries: one pass, O(1) average per lookup.

options.label: Sort, then binary search
options.rationale: Sorting costs O(n log n) first, and it is not the single pass the job needs.

options.label: Max-heap of amounts
options.rationale: A heap exposes only its largest entry; it cannot look up a specific partner amount.

scenarios.explanation: For each amount a, the partner must equal target - a. A hash map of amounts already seen answers 'is the partner here?' in O(1) on average, so a single pass finds a pair in O(n) time and O(n) space. It trades memory for the O(n^2) cost of testing every pair.

validations.question: One pass over n entries, one hash lookup each. What is the expected time to find a pair?
Target 9. Scan left to right, looking for each value's partner among earlier values. Tap the cell where a partner is first found.

scenarios.title: Live median response time
scenarios.prompt: A monitoring page shows the median response time of a request stream. New samples arrive constantly, and the median must be available right after each one, without re-sorting everything.

options.label: Re-sort after each sample
options.rationale: O(n log n) per sample, so the cost explodes as the stream grows.

options.label: One min-heap of all samples
options.rationale: Exposes only the minimum; reaching the middle means popping half the heap.

options.label: Insert into a sorted array
options.rationale: The median is an index read, but each insert shifts O(n) elements to keep the order.

options.label: Two heaps: max and min
options.rationale: A max-heap holds the smaller half and a min-heap the larger half; the median sits at the tops, and an insert is O(log n).

scenarios.explanation: Split the samples into two halves: a max-heap for the smaller half and a min-heap for the larger half, rebalanced so their sizes differ by at most one. The median is the top of the larger heap, or the mean of both tops. Adding a sample costs O(log n) and reading the median is O(1).

validations.question: Two-heap running median: cost of adding one sample and reading the median, with n samples so far?

scenarios.title: Cash-flow window finder
scenarios.prompt: Finance has 1M daily net cash-flow figures, positive or negative. Count the contiguous day ranges whose total equals exactly a target T. A sliding window fails here, and testing every range is too slow.

options.label: Two-pointer sliding window
options.rationale: Moving pointers by comparing the sum to T needs non-negative values; negatives break it.

options.label: Test every start and end
options.rationale: Even with a running sum per start, that is O(n^2) ranges, far too slow for 1M days.

options.label: Sort values, then scan
options.rationale: Sorting destroys the day order, and the ranges must be contiguous days.

options.label: Prefix sums + hash map
options.rationale: Counts earlier prefix sums equal to (current prefix - T) in O(1): one pass, O(n) time.

scenarios.explanation: Let P[i] be the running total after day i. A range sums to T exactly when P[j] - P[i] = T, so at each day j count the earlier prefixes equal to P[j] - T. A hash map from prefix value to count answers that in O(1) on average: one pass, O(n) time, O(n) space. Seed the map with 0 for ranges that start on day one.

validations.question: Prefix sums with a hash map over n daily figures, one lookup per day. What is the expected time?
Target 3. Scanning left to right, tap the first day on which some range ending there sums to 3.
